blocks.text: I’ve always been interested in what it is like to be someone else — how we experience the world, build our identities, and see ourselves. My background in psychology has deepened this curiosity and continues to influence the way I approach portraiture. With identical twins, that curiosity found a particularly interesting subject. They share so much, yet each person develops their own personality and way of being in the world. Their resemblance has a strong visual impact, but what interests me most are the small differences that emerge over time — the ways each person’s presence becomes visible within the shared image. Otherness is a long-term project that continues to grow. Finding identical twins willing to participate is not always easy, which gives the work a slower, more organic pace. Each new pair brings a different dynamic and adds another layer to the project, which is what keeps me returning to it — discovering the different ways twins express their connection while still remaining individuals. My process is quite intuitive. Every portrait is a collaboration between me and my subjects, and I try to create space for something to unfold rather than follow a rigid concept. The relationship between the twins often shapes the image as much as my own ideas do. At the same time, an essential part of my approach as a photographer has always been the desire to create beautiful images. For me, the conceptual and the aesthetic are not separate — they exist together and give the work its meaning.
